theme: Timothy; the Macedonian call; Lydia; the Philippian jailer
readingInstruction: Read Acts 16:1-40. Timothy joins Paul, a vision calls them to Macedonia, Lydia believes in Philippi, and a jailer is converted after an earthquake. Notice how each conversion looks different and how each family is included.
settingTheScene: The second missionary journey takes Paul and Silas through Asia Minor. In Lystra, they pick up Timothy, a young disciple of Jewish and Greek parentage. The Spirit forbids them to speak in Asia and Bithynia, and in a night vision, a man of Macedonia calls them to cross to Europe. The gospel reaches the continent for the first time at Philippi, a Roman colony.
observation: “Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek” (16:3).
“A man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, Come over to Macedonia and help us” (16:9).
“The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul” (16:14).
“About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them” (16:25).
“And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken” (16:26).
“Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (16:30).
“Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household” (16:31).
“He rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God” (16:34).
interpretation:
Timothy, whose mother is a believing Jew and whose father is Greek, is well spoken of. Paul circumcises him, not because it is necessary for salvation, as Acts 15 has just settled, but to avoid hindering the gospel among Jews. This shows Paul’s flexibility on matters of culture. Titus, a Gentile, was not circumcised under pressure (Galatians 2:3). The difference is the reason: Timothy’s circumcision was a choice for mission, not a requirement for salvation.

The vision leads them to Philippi. On the Sabbath, outside the gate by the river, they find women gathered to pray. Lydia, a dealer in purple goods and a worshiper of God, listens. “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.” Conversion is God’s work. She is baptized with her household and invites them to stay at her house.

Then a slave girl with a spirit of divination follows them, shouting. Paul commands the spirit to come out in the name of Jesus Christ. Her owners, who lost their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates. They are beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison with their feet in stocks. At midnight they are praying and singing hymns, and the prisoners are listening. A great earthquake shakes the prison, the doors open, and everyone’s chains come loose. The jailer, thinking the prisoners have escaped, is about to kill himself. Paul cries, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.” The jailer trembles, falls before Paul and Silas, and asks, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They answer, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

This is the clearest answer in the Bible to the question of how to be saved: believe in the Lord Jesus. Then they speak the word of the Lord to him and his household. That same night he washes their wounds and is baptized with all his family. He brings them into his house and sets food before them, “and rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God.” In the morning, the magistrates send word to release them, and Paul insists on a public apology, because he is a Roman citizen. This protects the young church.

Three conversions: a wealthy businesswoman, a slave girl freed from a spirit, and a rough jailer. The gospel crosses class and gender lines.
connection: 2 Timothy 1:5 and 3:14-15 describe Timothy’s heritage. Galatians 2:3-5 is Titus not circumcised. 1 Corinthians 9:19-23 explains Paul’s flexibility for the gospel. Philippians 1:1-11 is Paul’s letter to the same church. Romans 10:9-13 says if you confess with your mouth and believe in your heart, you will be saved. John 6:29 says to believe in him whom he has sent. 1 Peter 2:21-23 and 4:12-16 treat unjust suffering. Psalm 40:3 speaks of a new song.
application:
Memorize Acts 16:31. It is the memory verse of this week.

Sing a hymn tonight even if things are hard, as Paul did in prison.

Pray for the “household” in your life, that the whole family would believe.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to open your heart and the hearts of those you love.
Thank him for shaking prisons and setting captives free.
Tell him what you need to be set free from.
